name: Zeno of Citium
bio: A merchant from Cyprus who, after a shipwreck brought him to Athens, turned to philosophy. Around 300 BC he began teaching at the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, which gave the school its name. He taught that virtue is the only true good and that a good life means living in agreement with nature.

p: Zeno was born around 334 BC in Citium, a harbour town on Cyprus where Greek and Phoenician culture met. His father Mnaseas was a merchant, and Zeno followed him into the trade. Ancient writers describe him as tall, thin and dark-skinned, with a slight stoop and a habit of keeping to himself.

The story of how he became a philosopher was told for centuries. In his early thirties Zeno was carrying a cargo of purple dye from Phoenicia when his ship was wrecked near Piraeus, the port of Athens. Stranded in the city, he sat down in a bookshop and listened to the bookseller read from the second book of Xenophon's memoirs of Socrates. Zeno was so taken that he asked where men like that could be found. At that moment Crates the Cynic happened to walk past, and the bookseller pointed and said: "Follow that man." Zeno later joked that he had made a prosperous voyage on the day he was shipwrecked.

Crates taught him the Cynic way of life: plain clothes, little food, no shame about poverty and a sharp disregard for convention. Zeno admired the toughness but was too modest for some of the Cynic stunts, and Crates is said to have teased him for it. He went on to study logic with Stilpo of Megara and attended the lectures of Polemo, head of Plato's Academy. Polemo complained that Zeno slipped in through the garden gate, stole his doctrines and dressed them up in Phoenician clothes. That was close to the truth: Zeno built something new out of everything he had heard.

Around 300 BC Zeno began to teach in the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, a public colonnade on the north side of the Athenian Agora decorated with paintings of the Battle of Marathon. Anyone could walk in and listen. His followers were first called Zenonians and later simply Stoics, after the place where they met.

Zeno divided philosophy into three parts: logic, physics and ethics. The goal of life, he taught, is "to live in agreement", which his successors expanded to "living in agreement with nature". Virtue is the only true good and vice the only true evil. Health, wealth, reputation and even life itself are "indifferent": some are reasonably preferred, but none of them can make a person good or bad. Strong passions such as fear, craving and rage are errors of judgment that a trained mind can correct. The universe is ordered by reason, the logos, and a human being is a small part of that rational whole.

His early book, the Republic, sketched a Cynic-flavoured ideal society without temples, law courts or money, bound together by love and virtue. Later Stoics found it embarrassing and tried to explain it away.

Zeno lived on bread, figs, honey and water, and his frugality became proverbial: Athenians said someone was "more self-controlled than Zeno the philosopher". He disliked crowds and would sit at the end of a couch so that at least one side of him was free. He is credited with the remark that we have two ears and one mouth so that we may listen more and speak less.

King Antigonus II Gonatas of Macedon admired him, attended his lectures and invited him to court. Zeno, by then old, declined and sent his students Persaeus and Philonides instead. Athens honoured him with a public decree, a golden crown and a tomb at public cost, stating that he had made the young men who came to him better people and had lived a life that matched his teaching.

According to Diogenes Laertius, Zeno died around 262 BC after tripping as he left the school and breaking a toe. He struck the ground with his hand, quoted a line from a tragedy, "I come, why do you call me?", and held his breath until he died.
None of his writings survive except short fragments quoted by later authors. Yet every Stoic who followed, from Cleanthes to Marcus Aurelius, built on the house he founded.

name: Cleanthes
school: Stoic, second head of the Stoa
bio: A former boxer who earned his living drawing water at night so he could study with Zeno by day. He succeeded Zeno as head of the school. His Hymn to Zeus, one of the few early Stoic texts to survive complete, praises the reason that orders the world.

p: Cleanthes was born around 330 BC in Assos, a town in the Troad on the north-west coast of Asia Minor. Before philosophy he was a boxer. He arrived in Athens, so the story goes, with only four drachmas in his pocket, met Zeno and decided to stay.

To pay for his studies he worked at night drawing water for the city's gardens and kneading dough for a baker, which earned him the nickname Phreantles, "the Well-Filler". Because he seemed to have no visible means of support, he was once summoned before the Areopagus council to explain how he lived. He brought the gardener he worked for as his witness. The council was so impressed that it offered him ten minae as a gift, but Zeno told him not to accept it.

life.h: The slow student who carried the load
p: Cleanthes was not quick. Fellow students called him "the donkey", and he answered that he alone was strong enough to carry Zeno's burden. He compared himself to a hard writing tablet: difficult to write on, but it keeps what has been written. He was so poor that he took notes on oyster shells and the shoulder blades of oxen because he could not afford papyrus.
He studied under Zeno for nineteen years, and when Zeno died around 262 BC, Cleanthes became head of the Stoa. He led the school for more than thirty years.

Cleanthes' most famous work is the Hymn to Zeus, the longest piece of early Stoic writing that survives in full. It praises Zeus not as a bearded god on a mountain but as the reason that runs through the whole universe, steering everything and turning disorder into order. Only the bad, the hymn says, act against this order, and in doing so they harm themselves.

Another short poem of his became one of the best-known prayers in Stoic literature: "Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you have ordained for me. I will follow without hesitation; and if I am unwilling and become bad, I will follow anyway." Epictetus closed his Handbook with these lines, and Seneca translated them into Latin, adding his own famous line: "The fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling."

Cleanthes gave Stoic physics much of its vocabulary. He described the soul and the cosmos as held together by tension, a kind of inner tone, and he saw the sun as the ruling part of the universe. He wrote a commentary on Heraclitus, whose ideas about fire and the logos fed into Stoic thinking. He was also a strict moralist: he held that virtue, once acquired, cannot be lost, and that pleasure is not natural at all. Plutarch reports that he thought Aristarchus of Samos should be charged with impiety for suggesting that the earth moves around the sun.
He was less gifted at logic than at living. His own student Chrysippus is said to have told him: "Just give me the doctrines, I will find the proofs myself."

Cleanthes died around 230 BC in extreme old age; sources give his age as eighty or even ninety-nine. He had a sore on his gum, and his doctors told him to fast for two days. When the sore healed and they allowed him to eat again, he refused, saying that he had already come so far along the road. He kept fasting until he died, and Chrysippus succeeded him as head of the school.
What Cleanthes gave the Stoa was continuity. He was not its most original mind, but his patience, his poverty and his loyalty to Zeno kept the school alive through its first generation.

name: Chrysippus
school: Stoic, third head of the Stoa
bio: The great systematiser of Stoicism. He is said to have written more than 700 works, especially on logic, and the ancients said that without Chrysippus there would be no Stoa. Only fragments of his writing survive.

p: Chrysippus was born around 279 BC in Soli, a Greek city in Cilicia on the south coast of modern Turkey. As a young man he was a long-distance runner. After his inheritance was confiscated, he came to Athens and studied with Cleanthes, and for a time he also attended the Academy, where the sceptics Arcesilaus and Lacydes taught. That training in arguing both sides of a question shaped the rest of his life.

He was small, and a statue of him in the Kerameikos was said to be almost hidden behind a nearby equestrian statue, so the comic poets called him "Krysippus", the hidden one. The well-known type of his portrait shows him seated, leaning forward with one hand stretched out, as if counting arguments on his fingers.

Chrysippus became head of the Stoa after Cleanthes died around 230 BC. At that point the school was under heavy attack from the sceptical Academy, which argued that the Stoics could not show that any knowledge was certain. Chrysippus answered every objection and rebuilt Stoic teaching into a complete system. Ancient writers said: "If there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no Stoa." His opponent Carneades later turned the line around: "If there had been no Chrysippus, there would have been no me."
He is said to have written more than 705 books. Almost all of them are lost; we know his views from quotations by friends and enemies, and from charred papyrus rolls found at Herculaneum.

Chrysippus is one of the great logicians of the ancient world. Where Aristotle's logic dealt with terms such as "all men" and "some animals", Chrysippus worked with whole statements joined by "if", "and" and "or". He set out five basic forms of valid argument, such as "If it is day, it is light; it is day; therefore it is light", and showed how more complex arguments can be reduced to them. Modern propositional logic, developed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, rediscovered much of what he had already worked out.

Stoics believed that everything happens according to fate, a chain of causes running through the universe. Critics asked: if everything is fated, how can anyone be blamed or praised? Chrysippus answered with an image preserved by Cicero. Push a cylinder and it rolls; push a cone and it spins. The push starts the motion, but the shape of the object decides how it moves. Events in the world give us the push, but how we respond depends on our own character and judgment. That is where our responsibility lies.

Chrysippus also worked out the Stoic account of emotion. Fear, grief, craving and wild delight are not forces that overwhelm reason from outside; they are judgments that something bad or good is happening, followed by an excessive impulse. Because they are judgments, they can be examined and changed. His four books On the Passions became the basis for the Stoic "therapy of the soul" that Seneca and Epictetus later practised.

Chrysippus died around 206 BC, aged about seventy-three. Diogenes Laertius gives two stories. In one, he drank undiluted wine at a sacrifice, grew dizzy and died a few days later. In the other, he saw a donkey eating his figs, told an old woman to give the animal some neat wine to wash them down, and laughed so hard at his own joke that he died.
Whatever the truth, the Stoicism that Romans like Cato, Seneca and Marcus Aurelius received was, in its structure, the Stoicism of Chrysippus.

name: Zeno of Tarsus
school: Stoic, fourth head of the Stoa
bio: Pupil and successor of Chrysippus as head of the school. He wrote little but had many students. He is reported to have doubted the Stoic doctrine that the universe is periodically destroyed by fire.

p: Zeno of Tarsus was the fourth head of the Stoa. He was born in Tarsus in Cilicia, the same region as his teacher Chrysippus; some sources say his family came from Sidon in Phoenicia. His father was named Dioscorides. He came to Athens as a young man, studied under Chrysippus and took over the school when Chrysippus died around 206 BC.

He should not be confused with the founder, Zeno of Citium, who had died more than fifty years earlier. Ancient writers already had to keep apart several philosophers named Zeno, and Diogenes Laertius lists eight of them.

Very little survives about Zeno of Tarsus. Diogenes Laertius says he wrote only a few books but had a great many students. In other words, he seems to have been a teacher more than an author, someone who kept the school running after the towering output of Chrysippus.

One doctrine is linked with his name. The early Stoics believed that the universe goes through endless cycles: at the end of each one, everything returns to pure fire in a great "conflagration", and then the world is reborn exactly as before. Zeno of Tarsus is reported to have suspended judgment on this teaching. He did not reject it outright, but he would not affirm it either. It is the first sign of a more cautious attitude to Stoic physics that later heads of the school, such as Diogenes of Babylon and Panaetius, carried further.

No statue, bust or coin with a reliable identification of Zeno of Tarsus is known. That is why his challenge coin carries the gold Stoa column instead of a face: the column stands for the school itself, which he served as head.

None of his own words have come down to us. Any line attributed to him today should be treated with suspicion. For the Daily Thoughts app this means his page will mostly serve as a link in the chain from Chrysippus to Diogenes of Babylon, rather than as the source of one-pagers.

Zeno of Tarsus led the Stoa during a period when Athens was no longer a major political power but was still the intellectual capital of the Greek world. Rome was rising in the west and would soon reach into Greece itself. The school he handed on to Diogenes of Babylon was stable, respected and increasingly cautious about its boldest claims. That careful, practical Stoicism is the version that would soon travel to Rome and win over its elite.

name: Diogenes of Babylon
bio: Head of the Stoa in the second century BC. In 155 BC he went to Rome with the Athenian embassy of philosophers, and his lectures there helped bring Stoicism to the Romans. He wrote on ethics, language and music.

p: Diogenes was born around 230 BC in Seleucia on the Tigris, the great Greek city founded near ancient Babylon, which is why he was called "the Babylonian". He came to Athens, studied with Chrysippus and then with Zeno of Tarsus, and succeeded Zeno as head of the Stoa. He led the school for several decades and lived to over eighty.

Diogenes wrote on a wide range of subjects. His handbook On Voice set out the Stoic theory of language: sounds, letters, parts of speech and the difference between a mere noise and a meaningful word. It shaped Greek and Roman grammar for centuries. He also wrote On Music, arguing that music has real effects on character, a claim the Epicurean Philodemus later attacked point by point in a book whose remains were found at Herculaneum. In ethics he refined the Stoic idea of value, explaining how things that are not good in themselves, such as health or money, can still be rationally chosen.

Diogenes is best remembered for a journey to Rome. In 155 BC Athens was fined 500 talents for raiding the town of Oropus. To appeal, the Athenians sent three of their leading philosophers as ambassadors: Carneades of the Academy, Critolaus of the Peripatetic school and Diogenes for the Stoics.

While they waited for the Senate, the three men gave public lectures, and young Romans flocked to hear them. Carneades caused a scandal by speaking in praise of justice one day and arguing against it the next. Cato the Elder, alarmed that Greek cleverness would corrupt Roman youth, urged the Senate to settle the matter quickly and send the philosophers home. The fine was reduced to 100 talents. Ancient writers praised Diogenes in particular for his sober and restrained style of speaking. For many Romans, this was their first direct encounter with Greek philosophy, and with Stoicism in particular.

Cicero preserves a famous debate between Diogenes and his student Antipater. A merchant brings a cargo of grain to Rhodes during a famine. He knows that several other grain ships are on their way and will arrive soon. Must he tell the Rhodians, which will lower his price, or may he keep quiet and sell at the famine price?

Diogenes argued that the merchant must not lie, but he is not obliged to volunteer every piece of information that would help the buyer. Antipater argued that honesty requires full disclosure, because we are all members of one human community. The case is still discussed in business ethics today.

Diogenes taught many of the people who would carry Stoicism forward: Antipater of Tarsus, who succeeded him; Panaetius of Rhodes, who brought the school to the Roman elite; and Boethus of Sidon. He died around 150 to 140 BC.

No reliable portrait of Diogenes of Babylon exists, so his coin carries the gold Stoa column. Only fragments of his writings survive, quoted by Cicero, Philodemus and others, so genuine quotations are scarce.

name: Antipater of Tarsus
bio: Successor of Diogenes of Babylon and teacher of Panaetius. He is remembered for his debates with the sceptic Carneades and for his discussion of honesty in trade, which Cicero retold in On Duties.

p: Antipater was born in Tarsus in Cilicia and studied in Athens under Diogenes of Babylon. When Diogenes died, around the middle of the second century BC, Antipater became head of the Stoa. He led it until his death around 130 BC, when his student Panaetius took over.

Antipater's great opponent was Carneades, head of the sceptical Academy and one of the most brilliant debaters of the ancient world. Carneades attacked Stoic teaching in public lectures, and Antipater did not dare to face him in open argument. Instead he wrote book after book in reply. For this he was mocked as kalamoboas, "the pen-shouter", a man who shouted with his pen instead of his voice. Plutarch tells the story; it shows how much pressure the Stoics were under in this period.

Antipater worked hard on how to state the Stoic goal of life precisely. His versions run roughly: "to live continually choosing what is in accordance with nature and rejecting what is contrary to it", or "to do everything in one's power, continuously and without wavering, to obtain the things that are by nature preferred".

The point is subtle but important. The Stoic does aim at real things in the world: health, safety for family, success in a task. But what makes the life good is the skill and steadiness of the aiming, not whether the target is actually hit. Cicero later used the image of an archer: the archer does everything possible to hit the mark, yet the goal is to shoot well, not merely to strike the target. This distinction between doing your part and controlling the outcome is at the heart of later Stoic practice.

In the debate about the merchant who brings grain to Rhodes during a famine, knowing that other ships are coming, Antipater took the strict line against his teacher Diogenes. Because all people belong to one community, he argued, the merchant must tell the buyers everything he knows. Hiding the truth for profit is not compatible with honesty, even if no direct lie is told. Cicero, who reports the case, sides with Antipater.

A long fragment of Antipater's essay On Marriage survives in the anthology of Stobaeus. It argues that marriage and raising children are among the most necessary and fitting duties of a good citizen, and describes marriage as a full partnership in which husband and wife share body, soul and property. This warm view of family life was taken up by later Stoics such as Musonius Rufus.
No portrait of Antipater is known, so his coin shows the gold Stoa column. His works survive only in fragments, which means that there are very few direct quotes that can safely be attributed to him.

name: Panaetius of Rhodes
bio: Friend of Scipio Aemilianus and a central figure in bringing Stoicism into Roman public life. He softened the school's strict teaching to speak to people making progress rather than only to the perfect sage. Cicero's On Duties draws heavily on his work.

p: Panaetius was born around 185 BC into a leading family of Lindos on the island of Rhodes. His education was wide. He studied in Pergamon with Crates of Mallos, the famous scholar of Homer, and then in Athens under the Stoics Diogenes of Babylon and Antipater of Tarsus.

In the 140s BC Panaetius went to Rome and became a close friend of Scipio Aemilianus, the general who had destroyed Carthage in 146 BC. He belonged to the circle around Scipio that included the statesman Laelius and the Greek historian Polybius. When Scipio led an embassy to Egypt and the eastern kingdoms around 140 to 139 BC, Panaetius travelled with him.

Through these friendships, Stoicism found a home in the Roman ruling class. Panaetius showed Romans who led armies and governed provinces that Stoic ethics could be a practical guide for public life, not just a doctrine for sages.
When Antipater died around 129 BC, Panaetius became head of the school in Athens and led it for twenty years until his death around 109 BC. Historians see him as the start of the "Middle Stoa".

He softened several of the school's harder positions. He doubted the doctrine that the world would end in a great conflagration, rejected most forms of divination and astrology, and spoke with admiration of Plato and Aristotle. Instead of focusing on the perfect sage, who may never exist, he wrote for the person who is making progress: someone who is not yet wise but is trying to do better each day.

Panaetius' best-known idea is that each of us plays four roles, or personae. The first is our shared human nature as rational beings. The second is our individual nature: our talents, temperament and strengths. The third is the situation that chance has placed us in, such as wealth, family and political circumstance. The fourth is the role we choose for ourselves, such as a career or a way of life. A good life, he argued, respects all four. We should not try to imitate someone else's nature, but should act well as the particular person we are.

His most influential book was On Appropriate Action. It dealt with everyday duties: what a person owes to family, friends, country and themselves, and how to decide when these seem to clash. The book itself is lost, but Cicero used it as the model for the first two books of his own De Officiis, written in 44 BC. Through Cicero, Panaetius' practical ethics shaped the moral education of Europe for well over a thousand years.

Among his students were Posidonius of Apamea, who became the most learned Stoic of his age, and Hecato of Rhodes. Panaetius is said to have declined honorary Athenian citizenship, remarking that one city was enough for a sensible man.
No authentic portrait of Panaetius is known, so his coin carries the gold Stoa column. His words survive mostly in Cicero's Latin retelling rather than as direct quotations.

name: Cato the Younger
bio: Roman senator famous for his integrity and his opposition to Julius Caesar. He lived his Stoicism in public life rather than writing it down. After Caesar's victory he took his own life at Utica rather than accept Caesar's pardon, and later Stoics held him up as a model.

p: Marcus Porcius Cato was born in 95 BC, the great-grandson of Cato the Elder, the famously severe censor. Orphaned as a child, he grew up in the house of his uncle Marcus Livius Drusus. Plutarch says he was stubborn and serious even as a boy. When the dictator Sulla's men were killing political enemies, the young Cato asked his tutor for a sword so he could free Rome from tyranny.

He studied Stoic philosophy with Antipater of Tyre and later kept the Stoic Athenodorus Cordylion in his own household. He trained himself in hardship: walking bareheaded in heat and rain, travelling on foot while his friends rode, and dressing in a plain dark toga instead of the fashionable purple.

As military tribune in Macedonia in 67 BC, he shared the work and food of his soldiers. As quaestor in 64 BC he took control of the treasury, refused to pay out false claims and made the clerks who had grown rich on fraud answer for it. He became known as the one man in Rome who could not be bribed.

In December 63 BC the Senate debated what to do with the arrested conspirators of Catiline. Julius Caesar argued for life imprisonment. Cato replied with a speech so forceful that the Senate voted for execution. The historian Sallust later contrasted the two men: Caesar won glory by giving, Cato by refusing.

For the rest of his life Cato opposed the men who were turning the Republic into a contest of personal power: Pompey, Crassus and above all Caesar. He used every legal tool, including speaking until sunset to block votes. In 58 BC his enemies sent him away to annex Cyprus. He collected the royal treasure and brought nearly 7,000 talents back to Rome, with accounts so careful that he kept two copies. Both were lost on the way, one in a shipwreck and one in a fire.

When civil war broke out in 49 BC, Cato sided with Pompey as the lesser danger. After Caesar's victory at Pharsalus in 48 BC, Cato led the surviving troops on a long march across the Libyan desert on foot to join the republican forces in Africa. He took command of the city of Utica.

In April 46 BC Caesar crushed the republicans at Thapsus. Cato arranged ships for everyone in Utica who wanted to escape, then spent the night reading Plato's Phaedo, the dialogue about the death of Socrates and the immortality of the soul. He stabbed himself with his sword. His doctors found him still alive and bandaged the wound, but he tore it open and died. When Caesar heard, he said: "Cato, I begrudge you your death, as you begrudged me the saving of your life."

Cato left no writings except one speech, but he became the Stoic hero in action. Seneca returned to him again and again as the model of a man who could not be broken. Lucan made him the moral centre of his poem on the civil war. Dante placed him as guardian of the shores of Purgatory. Joseph Addison's play Cato (1713) was a favourite of George Washington, who had it performed for his army at Valley Forge in 1778.

name: Seneca
bio: Philosopher, playwright and adviser to the emperor Nero. His Letters to Lucilius and essays such as On the Shortness of Life are among the most widely read Stoic writings. Accused of conspiracy, he was ordered by Nero to take his own life.

p: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was born around 4 BC in Corduba, in the Roman province of Hispania, today Córdoba in Spain. His father, Seneca the Elder, was a wealthy writer on rhetoric. One of his brothers, Gallio, appears in the Acts of the Apostles as the governor before whom Paul was brought in Corinth.

Seneca was taken to Rome as a child. He suffered from poor health all his life, probably asthma or a lung disease, and spent several years recovering in Egypt with his aunt. As a young man he studied philosophy with the Stoic Attalus and with Sotion and Papirius Fabianus of the Sextii, a short-lived Roman school that combined Stoic and Pythagorean ideas. For a while he even gave up meat.

Seneca made his name as an orator and senator. According to later writers, the emperor Caligula was so jealous of his speaking that he nearly had him killed. In AD 41 the new emperor Claudius exiled him to Corsica, accused of adultery with Julia Livilla, the emperor's niece. He spent eight years on the island and wrote consolations to his mother Helvia and to the court official Polybius, both meditations on how to bear misfortune.

In AD 49 Agrippina, Claudius' new wife, recalled Seneca to tutor her son Nero. When Nero became emperor in 54 at the age of sixteen, Seneca and the praetorian prefect Burrus guided the government. The first five years of Nero's reign were later remembered as a time of good rule.

Then came compromise. Nero had his mother murdered in 59, and Seneca wrote the letter to the Senate justifying it. He also became enormously rich, with a fortune Tacitus put at 300 million sesterces, and critics called him a hypocrite who preached poverty from a palace. Seneca answered in On the Happy Life: the wise person may own wealth, as long as wealth does not own them.

After Burrus died in 62, Seneca's position became dangerous. He asked to retire, offered Nero his fortune, and withdrew from public life. In these last years he wrote his greatest work, the 124 Letters to Lucilius, along with Natural Questions. Earlier works include On Anger, On the Shortness of Life, On Tranquility of Mind and On Providence. He also wrote tragedies, such as Medea, Thyestes and Phaedra, which later shaped Elizabethan drama.

In AD 65 a plot to kill Nero, the Pisonian conspiracy, was discovered. Seneca was probably not involved, but Nero ordered him to die. Tacitus describes the scene. Seneca told his weeping friends that he was leaving them the one thing he still had, the pattern of his life. He opened his veins, but because he was old and thin the blood flowed slowly. He took poison, which did not work, and finally was carried into a hot bath, where he died. His wife Paulina tried to die with him but was saved on Nero's orders.

Seneca is the most readable of the Stoics. His letters are short, practical and personal, full of everyday scenes and striking lines. Early Christian writers admired him so much that a fake correspondence between Seneca and Saint Paul circulated for centuries. Montaigne, Shakespeare's contemporaries and modern readers have all returned to him for practical advice on time, anger, grief and fear.

name: Musonius Rufus
bio: Roman Stoic teacher, exiled several times by emperors, and the teacher of Epictetus. His lectures, preserved by his students, stress practice over theory and argue that women are just as capable of philosophy as men.

life.h: A Roman knight who taught in Greek
p: Gaius Musonius Rufus was born before AD 30 in Volsinii, an old Etruscan town in central Italy, today Bolsena. He belonged to the equestrian order, the class of Roman knights just below the senators. He taught philosophy in Rome, in Greek, and became so respected that later writers called him "the Roman Socrates".

In AD 65, after the Pisonian conspiracy against Nero, Musonius was exiled to Gyara, a barren, waterless island in the Aegean used as a prison for political enemies. People still sailed out to visit him and hear him teach. A later story says he discovered a spring on the island, making it more livable. He was recalled after Nero's death in 68.

In 69, the year of the four emperors, armies were marching on Rome. Musonius joined a delegation of senators sent to meet the troops of Vespasian's general outside the city. He walked among the soldiers lecturing on the blessings of peace and the dangers of war. Tacitus says the soldiers mocked him and he barely escaped being beaten.

In 70 he prosecuted Publius Egnatius Celer, a Stoic who had given false testimony that led to the death of the senator Barea Soranus, and won. When Vespasian expelled philosophers from Rome in 71, Musonius was at first allowed to stay, but he was later exiled again and returned only under the emperor Titus.

Musonius wrote nothing himself. His teaching survives through notes taken by a student named Lucius, preserved as some twenty-one short lectures, along with sayings quoted by later writers. They are practical and direct. Philosophy, he said, is useless unless it changes how you live, just as medicine is useless unless it heals. Virtue is not only known but trained, through hardship, simple food, cold and heat, and steady practice.

Musonius held views that were unusual in Rome. He argued that women have the same capacity for reason and virtue as men and should study philosophy. Daughters should receive the same education as sons. Marriage should be a full partnership of two people who share everything and care for each other. He taught that men as well as women should limit sex to marriage, opposed the common practice of abandoning unwanted newborns, and praised large families.

He recommended plain food, mostly vegetables, grains, fruit and cheese, prepared simply. He thought clothes and houses should protect the body, not display wealth, and that farming was a fitting occupation for a philosopher, because it kept body and mind healthy and left time to teach.

His most famous student was Epictetus, who heard him while still a slave and quotes him with deep respect in the Discourses. Another was the orator Dio Chrysostom. Through Epictetus, Musonius' style of practical, demanding Stoicism reached Marcus Aurelius.

No reliable portrait of Musonius is known, so his coin carries the gold Stoa column. The lecture notes of Lucius do give us his ideas in some detail, so short quotations from them can be used for one-pagers.

name: Epictetus
bio: Born a slave, he studied under Musonius Rufus and was later freed. After philosophers were expelled from Rome he taught at Nicopolis in Greece. His student Arrian recorded his teaching in the Discourses and the Handbook, built around one idea: separate what is up to us from what is not.

p: Epictetus was born around AD 50 in Hierapolis, a city in Phrygia in modern Turkey. He was born into slavery, and his name simply means "acquired". His mother was a slave, and we do not know his birth name. As a boy he came to Rome as the property of Epaphroditus, a powerful freedman who served as secretary to the emperor Nero.

Epictetus was lame. One story, told by the Christian writer Origen, says his master once twisted his leg to test him. Epictetus calmly warned that the leg would break, and when it did, he said only: "Didn't I tell you it would break?" Another source says the lameness came from rheumatism. Either way, it became part of his legend.

While still a slave, Epictetus was allowed to attend the lectures of Musonius Rufus, the leading Stoic teacher in Rome. Musonius trained him hard. Epictetus later recalled how Musonius would point out his faults so precisely that each student felt the lecture was aimed at him alone. At some point after Nero's death in 68, Epictetus was freed and began teaching philosophy himself.

Around 93 or 94 the emperor Domitian expelled all philosophers from Rome. Epictetus moved to Nicopolis, a city on the west coast of Greece, and opened a school that attracted young men from across the empire, many from wealthy Roman families. The emperor Hadrian is said to have visited him.

He lived with very little: a bed, a mat and a lamp. When his iron lamp was stolen, he bought a clay one and said the thief would have to become a thief again to take the next one. Late in life he took in a child whose parents were going to abandon it, and asked a woman to help him raise it.

Epictetus wrote nothing. A student, the historian Arrian of Nicomedia, took notes on his lectures and published them as the Discourses. Four of the original eight books survive. Arrian also produced a short summary, the Enchiridion or Handbook, meant to be kept close at hand.

The Handbook opens with the idea at the core of his teaching: "Some things are up to us and others are not." Our judgments, our desires, our choices and our actions are up to us. Our body, possessions, reputation and position are not. Freedom and peace come from caring about the first group and accepting the second. What disturbs us, he said, is not events but our judgments about them.

Marcus Aurelius was introduced to Epictetus' notes by his teacher Junius Rusticus and quotes him throughout the Meditations. Christian monks adapted the Handbook as a guide for monastic life. In the twentieth century, the psychologist Albert Ellis cited Epictetus as an inspiration for cognitive therapy. James Stockdale, a US Navy pilot held as a prisoner of war in Hanoi for over seven years, said Epictetus' teaching kept him alive.
Epictetus died around AD 135 in Nicopolis. The portrait on his coin is an imaginary one from an engraving printed in Oxford in 1715, since no portrait made from life exists.

name: Junius Rusticus
bio: Stoic philosopher, twice consul and Prefect of Rome, and the teacher Marcus Aurelius thanks most warmly in Book 1 of the Meditations. It was Rusticus who lent the young Marcus his own copy of Epictetus.

p: Quintus Junius Rusticus was born around AD 100 into a Roman senatorial family with a strong Stoic tradition. He was very probably the grandson of Arulenus Rusticus, a Stoic senator who was executed by the emperor Domitian in 93 for writing a book in praise of Thrasea Paetus, another Stoic who had died resisting Nero. For the Rustici, Stoicism was not an academic subject but a family inheritance, tied to the memory of men who had paid with their lives for speaking freely.

Rusticus became the most important philosophy teacher of the young Marcus Aurelius. In the first book of the Meditations, where Marcus thanks the people who shaped him, the entry for Rusticus is one of the longest. From him, Marcus writes, he learned:

that his character needed training and correction; not to be carried away by the showy rhetoric of the sophists, nor to write treatises on abstract topics or give moralising little speeches; not to parade about the house in formal dress; to write letters simply, like the one Rusticus wrote to Marcus' mother from Sinuessa; to be ready to forgive and be reconciled with those who had offended him as soon as they wanted to make peace; to read carefully and not be satisfied with a rough idea of a thing; and not to agree too quickly with people who talk a lot.

Most important of all, Rusticus lent Marcus his own copy of the notes of Epictetus' lectures. That gift set the direction of Marcus' inner life, and Epictetus is the philosopher Marcus quotes most often.

Rusticus was not only a teacher. He held high offices of state, serving as consul for the second time in 162, an honour Marcus gave to very few, and as urban prefect of Rome, in charge of order in the capital, from about 162 to 168. Marcus consulted him on both public and private matters.

As urban prefect, Rusticus presided over the trial of the Christian philosopher Justin Martyr and several companions around 165. The record of the trial, the Acts of Justin, preserves their exchange. Justin refused to sacrifice to the gods, and Rusticus, following the law as it stood, sentenced him to death. The episode is a reminder that a Stoic magistrate could still enforce the harsh laws of his time.
Rusticus died around 170. According to a later biography of Marcus, the emperor asked the Senate to set up statues in his honour and showed him a respect he gave to few others.

No portrait of Junius Rusticus is known, so his coin carries the gold Stoa column. He left no writings that have survived. What we know of his teaching comes almost entirely from Marcus' grateful memory, so any one-pager for Rusticus would start from Meditations 1.7 rather than his own words.

name: Marcus Aurelius
bio: Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and the last of the Five Good Emperors. He spent most of his reign on campaign along the Danube while the Antonine Plague swept the empire. His private notebook, the Meditations, was written in Greek and never meant for publication.

quotes.text: What stands in the way becomes the way.

life.h: A boy noticed by an emperor
p: Marcus Annius Verus was born in Rome on 26 April AD 121 into a wealthy family of Spanish origin. His father died when he was about three, and he was raised by his mother Domitia Lucilla and his grandfather. The emperor Hadrian took an interest in the serious, honest boy and nicknamed him Verissimus, "the most truthful", a play on his family name.

In 138, shortly before his death, Hadrian adopted Antoninus Pius as his heir, on the condition that Antoninus in turn adopt the seventeen-year-old Marcus and the young Lucius Verus. From that day Marcus was being prepared for the throne.

life.h: Education and the turn to philosophy
p: Marcus had the best teachers of his age. Marcus Cornelius Fronto, the most famous orator in Rome, taught him rhetoric, and their letters survive. But in his twenties Marcus turned more and more to philosophy. His Stoic teacher Junius Rusticus gave him the notes of Epictetus' lectures, and the first book of the Meditations thanks a long list of people, from family members to philosophers, for the qualities he learned from each.
In 145 he married Faustina, the daughter of Antoninus Pius. They had at least thirteen children, many of whom died young.

When Antoninus died in 161, Marcus became emperor and insisted that Lucius Verus rule with him as co-emperor. Almost at once, the empire was at war with Parthia in the east. The returning army brought back a devastating epidemic, the Antonine Plague, which killed millions across the empire over the following years.

From around 166, Germanic and Sarmatian peoples, among them the Marcomanni and Quadi, broke across the Danube frontier and even reached northern Italy. In 169 Lucius Verus died, and Marcus faced the crisis alone. With the treasury empty, he auctioned off palace treasures, including gold and crystal tableware, silk garments and jewels from the imperial household, in the Forum of Trajan rather than raise taxes on the provinces. This is the event behind the one-pager on Meditations 5.20.

Marcus spent most of the 170s with his armies on the Danube, at bases such as Carnuntum and Sirmium. There, in camp, he wrote private notes to himself in Greek. Later generations called them the Meditations; the oldest title is simply "To Himself". One book ends with the note "among the Quadi, on the Granua"; another, "at Carnuntum". They were never meant for publication. They are reminders to himself: to do the work in front of him, to be patient with difficult people, to remember that everything passes, and to act for the common good.

In 175 the general Avidius Cassius, believing a false rumour that Marcus had died, declared himself emperor. The revolt collapsed within months. Marcus burned Cassius' letters unread so he would not learn which friends had been involved.
Marcus died on 17 March 180, near the Danube front, probably at Vindobona (Vienna) or Sirmium. His son Commodus succeeded him and quickly abandoned his father's wars and values.

Marcus is remembered as the last of the "Five Good Emperors", a phrase popularised by Machiavelli and later by Edward Gibbon. His bronze equestrian statue survived in Rome because people believed it showed Constantine, the first Christian emperor. The Meditations survived in a single manuscript tradition and were first printed in 1559. Today they are the most widely read work of Stoic philosophy, and the motto of Stoic Ranger, "Impedimentum fit via", comes from them.

name: Socrates
bio: The Athenian who wrote nothing and questioned everyone. Through his students, Plato above all, he became the model of the examined life. Condemned to death for impiety and corrupting the young, he drank the hemlock rather than give up philosophy. The Stoics saw him as their great forerunner.

p: Socrates was born around 470 BC in Athens, in the district of Alopeke. His father Sophroniscus was a stonemason or sculptor, and his mother Phaenarete was a midwife. Socrates later described himself as a midwife of ideas: he did not give birth to wisdom himself, but helped others bring their own thoughts into the light and test whether they were sound.

He was famously ugly by Athenian standards, with a snub nose, bulging eyes and a thick neck, and he walked barefoot in all weathers. He married Xanthippe, who became proverbial as a difficult wife, and they had three sons.

Socrates served as a hoplite, a heavy infantryman, in the Peloponnesian War. At the siege of Potidaea he saved the life of the young Alcibiades and then gave up the prize for bravery to him. Alcibiades later described how Socrates stood still in thought from one dawn to the next, and how he endured the bitter northern winter in his ordinary cloak. During the retreat after the defeat at Delium in 424 BC, Socrates walked away calmly, so composed that no enemy dared attack him.

A friend, Chaerephon, asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer was: no one. Socrates was puzzled, because he knew he was not wise. He went around questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen, people with a reputation for wisdom, and found that they thought they knew things they did not. He concluded that his only advantage was that he knew he did not know.

His method was to ask questions. What is courage? What is justice? What is a good life? He would take a person's answer, draw out its consequences and show that it led to contradictions, leaving both of them to search further. He said that the unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.

Twice Socrates risked his life by refusing to do wrong. In 406 BC, when the Assembly wanted to try a group of generals together illegally, he alone refused to put the motion to a vote. In 404 BC the oligarchic regime of the Thirty ordered him and four others to arrest an innocent man, Leon of Salamis. The others went; Socrates simply went home.

In 399 BC Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting the young. His defence, as Plato records it in the Apology, refused to beg for mercy. He was convicted by a narrow margin. Asked to propose a penalty, he suggested free meals at public expense, as a reward for his service to the city. The jury sentenced him to death.

Friends arranged an escape, but Socrates refused, arguing in Plato's Crito that he would not break the laws of the city that had raised him. In prison he spent his last day discussing the immortality of the soul, then drank the hemlock calmly. His last words were: "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. Pay it and do not forget."

Socrates wrote nothing. We know him through Plato, Xenophon and the comic poet Aristophanes. For the Stoics he was the closest thing to a real sage. Epictetus quotes him more than any other philosopher, and Zeno's path to philosophy began with a book about him.

name: Plato
bio: Student of Socrates and founder of the Academy in Athens. His dialogues, with Socrates as the main speaker, range over justice, love, knowledge and the soul, and have shaped Western thought ever since. The four cardinal virtues the Stoics adopted are set out in his Republic.

p: Plato was born around 428 BC in Athens into one of the city's oldest aristocratic families. Ancient tradition says his real name was Aristocles and that "Plato", meaning "broad", was a nickname, perhaps for his shoulders, his forehead or his style. As a young man he may have wrestled and written poetry. Two of his relatives, Critias and Charmides, were among the Thirty, the oligarchs who ruled Athens by terror in 404 BC. Their violence turned him away from a political career.

Plato became one of the young men around Socrates. Socrates' execution in 399 BC, when Plato was about twenty-eight, was the turning point of his life. It convinced him that no city could be just until philosophers became rulers or rulers became philosophers. Almost all of his writings give Socrates the leading role.

After Socrates' death Plato left Athens and travelled, to Megara, perhaps to Egypt, and to southern Italy, where he met Pythagorean thinkers such as Archytas of Tarentum. Around 388 BC he visited the court of Dionysius I, tyrant of Syracuse. According to a later story, the visit ended badly and Plato was sold into slavery on the island of Aegina, until a man named Anniceris bought his freedom.

Later in life he went to Syracuse twice more, in 367 and 361 BC, at the urging of his friend Dion, hoping to turn the young ruler Dionysius II into a philosopher-king. Both attempts failed, and Plato was lucky to get home.

Around 387 BC Plato founded a school in a grove sacred to the hero Akademos, just outside the walls of Athens. The Academy taught mathematics, astronomy, politics and philosophy, and it lasted in some form until Sulla's army sacked Athens in 86 BC. Aristotle studied there for twenty years. Zeno, the founder of Stoicism, attended lectures there under Polemo.

Plato wrote philosophy as drama: conversations in which characters argue their way toward the truth. All of his roughly thirty-five dialogues have survived, among them the Apology, Crito and Phaedo on Socrates' trial and death, the Symposium on love, the Republic on justice and the ideal city, the Timaeus on the creation of the world, and the Laws, his last and longest work.

His central ideas include the theory of Forms, the belief that behind the changing things we see stand perfect, unchanging realities such as Justice and Beauty; the division of the soul into reason, spirit and appetite; and the four cardinal virtues of wisdom, courage, moderation and justice. The Stoics took over these four virtues as the core of their ethics. His allegory of the cave, in which prisoners mistake shadows for reality, is one of the most famous images in philosophy.

Plato died around 348 BC at about eighty and was buried in the Academy. The philosopher Alfred North Whitehead later wrote that the whole European philosophical tradition is a series of footnotes to Plato. The Stoics disagreed with him on many points, but they argued in a world he had shaped.

name: Aristotle
bio: Student of Plato, tutor of Alexander the Great and founder of the Lyceum. He wrote on nearly every field of knowledge, from logic and biology to ethics and politics. His Nicomachean Ethics describes virtue as a habit and the good life as human flourishing.

p: Aristotle was born in 384 BC in Stagira, a small Greek town in the Chalcidice peninsula of northern Greece. His father Nicomachus was the court physician of King Amyntas III of Macedon, the grandfather of Alexander the Great. Both parents died when he was young, and he was raised by a guardian.

At seventeen Aristotle went to Athens and joined Plato's Academy. He stayed for twenty years, first as a student and then as a teacher, until Plato's death in 347 BC. Plato is said to have called him "the mind of the school". Aristotle admired his teacher, but came to reject the theory of Forms; in a famous line, he said that Plato was dear to him, but truth was dearer.

After leaving Athens, Aristotle spent several years in Assos, at the court of the ruler Hermias, whose niece Pythias he married, and then on the island of Lesbos. There, with his friend Theophrastus, he made close studies of marine animals, careful observations that made him the founder of biology as a science.

In 343 BC King Philip II of Macedon invited him to tutor his thirteen-year-old son Alexander. Aristotle taught him for several years at Mieza, a quiet sanctuary of the Nymphs. How much of Aristotle's thinking rubbed off on the future conqueror is debated, but Alexander is said to have slept with a copy of the Iliad annotated by his teacher.

In 335 BC Aristotle returned to Athens and founded his own school in the Lyceum, a gymnasium sacred to Apollo Lyceius. He liked to teach while walking along its covered walkways, and his followers became known as the Peripatetics, "those who walk around". The school collected books, gathered information on the constitutions of 158 Greek cities and organised research in almost every field.

The works that survive are mostly his lecture notes, which is why they can be dense and dry. They cover an astonishing range: logic in the Organon, nature in the Physics, first principles in the Metaphysics, the soul in On the Soul, animals, politics, rhetoric and poetry. His Nicomachean Ethics argues that the goal of life is eudaimonia, flourishing, achieved through virtues of character built up by habit, each of them a mean between two extremes, such as courage between cowardice and recklessness.
Here the Stoics parted ways with him. Aristotle held that a good life also needs some external goods, such as health, friends and a measure of wealth. The Stoics insisted that virtue alone is enough.

When Alexander died in 323 BC, anti-Macedonian feeling exploded in Athens and Aristotle was charged with impiety. Remembering Socrates, he left the city, saying he would not let the Athenians sin twice against philosophy. He died the following year, in 322 BC, at Chalcis on the island of Euboea, aged about sixty-two.

His works were edited in the first century BC by Andronicus of Rhodes, preserved by Arab and Byzantine scholars and rediscovered in Western Europe in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Medieval writers simply called him "the Philosopher". For nearly two thousand years, logic, natural science and ethics were studied in the framework he built.

name: Heraclitus
bio: Known as the Obscure for his riddling sayings. He taught that everything is in flux, held together by a hidden order he called the logos. The Stoics took over his logos and his fire as the basis of their physics.

p: Heraclitus lived around 535 to 475 BC in Ephesus, a rich Greek city on the coast of Ionia in modern Turkey. He came from an old aristocratic family that held the hereditary title of "king", a priestly office. According to Diogenes Laertius, Heraclitus gave the title up in favour of his brother.

He was proud, solitary and contemptuous of nearly everyone. He mocked Homer, Hesiod and Pythagoras, and said that learning many things does not teach understanding. When the people of Ephesus exiled his friend Hermodorus, Heraclitus declared that all the adult Ephesians should hang themselves and leave the city to the boys. One story says he withdrew from public life to play dice with children at the temple of Artemis, telling the citizens that this was better than taking part in their politics.

Heraclitus wrote a single book, which he is said to have deposited in the great temple of Artemis at Ephesus. It is lost, but around 130 short fragments survive, quoted by later writers. They are written in compressed, riddling sentences, which earned him the nickname "the Obscure". Socrates is said to have remarked that what he understood of the book was excellent, and what he did not understand was probably excellent too, but it would take a diver from Delos to get to the bottom of it.

Heraclitus taught that there is a single law or reason, the logos, which governs everything, though most people do not notice it, living as if asleep. The world is like an ever-living fire, kindling and going out in measures. Everything is in constant change, and the world holds together through the tension of opposites, like a bow or a lyre. "The road up and the road down are one and the same." Plato summed up his view with the famous image that you cannot step into the same river twice, because new waters are always flowing.
He also wrote that "character is a person's fate", a line Stoics would have agreed with.

The Stoics took more from Heraclitus than from almost any other early thinker. Zeno and Cleanthes adopted his ideas of a rational logos running through the universe and of fire as its basic element. Cleanthes wrote a commentary on his book. Marcus Aurelius quotes him several times in the Meditations, including the warning not to act and speak like people asleep.

Diogenes Laertius tells that Heraclitus fell ill with dropsy, buried himself in cow dung in the hope that its warmth would draw out the fluid, and died. The story is probably invented, like many ancient philosophers' deaths.

Later tradition paired him with Democritus as "the weeping philosopher", who mourned the folly of the world, while Democritus laughed at it. The portrait on his coin comes from a painting of this weeping Heraclitus by the Dutch artist Johannes Moreelse, made around 1630. No portrait made in his lifetime survives.

name: Miyamoto Musashi
bio: Japan's most famous swordsman, said to have been undefeated in more than sixty duels. In his last years he retired to a cave and wrote The Book of Five Rings on strategy and self-discipline. He was also an accomplished painter and calligrapher.

p: Miyamoto Musashi was born around 1584 in western Japan, probably in Harima or Mimasaka province. His childhood name was Bennosuke, and his family was connected to the Shinmen clan. He grew up at the end of more than a century of civil war in Japan, when skill with the sword could still decide a man's future.

By his own account in The Book of Five Rings, he fought his first duel at thirteen, defeating a samurai named Arima Kihei. At sixteen he beat a strong opponent from Tajima. He may have fought at the great Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, though which side he was on is unclear.

Around 1604 Musashi went to Kyoto and challenged the Yoshioka family, famous sword teachers to the Ashikaga shoguns. According to tradition he defeated the head of the school and his brother, and then a large group of Yoshioka students who tried to ambush him.

His most famous duel took place in 1612 on Funashima, a small island in the strait between Honshu and Kyushu, now known as Ganryū-jima. His opponent was Sasaki Kojirō, a celebrated swordsman known for an unusually long blade. As the story is usually told, Musashi arrived late, having carved a wooden sword from a boat's oar on the way, and killed Kojirō with a single blow. Many details were added by later storytellers, but the duel made Musashi a legend.
He wrote that he fought more than sixty duels by the age of thirty and never lost.

life.h: Two swords and the way of strategy
p: Musashi developed a style of fighting with two swords at once, the long sword and the short one, which he called Niten Ichi-ryū, the "two heavens as one" school. But he insisted that strategy was more than swordsmanship. The same principles of timing, rhythm, observation and adapting to circumstances applied to a duel between two men and a battle between armies, and to any craft practised seriously.

In later life Musashi became an accomplished artist. His ink paintings, such as Shrike on a Withered Branch and Hotei Watching a Cockfight, are treasured in Japan for their spare, decisive brushwork. He also produced calligraphy and wood carvings. He took part in the suppression of the Shimabara Rebellion in 1637 to 1638, where he was injured by a stone.
In 1640 the lord Hosokawa Tadatoshi invited him to Kumamoto on the island of Kyushu. In 1643 Musashi withdrew to a cave called Reigandō in the nearby mountains to write.

The result was Go Rin no Sho, The Book of Five Rings, organised into five scrolls named Earth, Water, Fire, Wind and Void. It is a manual of strategy, but also a guide to discipline and clear perception. Its list of basic principles opens with "Do not think dishonestly" and "The Way is in training". A week before his death in 1645 he wrote the Dokkōdō, "The Way of Walking Alone", twenty-one short precepts for self-discipline, among them "Accept everything just the way it is" and "Do not regret what you have done".

Musashi has no historical link to the Stoics, but his focus on training, self-command and acceptance of what cannot be changed makes him a natural companion to them. The portrait on his coin is traditionally regarded as a self-portrait.

name: Sun Tzu
bio: The general traditionally credited with The Art of War. Whether one man wrote it or it grew over generations is debated, but its lessons on preparation, deception and winning without fighting are still studied by soldiers and business leaders.

p: According to tradition, Sun Tzu, "Master Sun", was a man named Sun Wu who lived around 544 to 496 BC, at the end of China's Spring and Autumn period. He is said to have come from the state of Qi and to have served King Helü of Wu, a rising state in the lower Yangtze region, as a general.

The earliest account of his life comes from the historian Sima Qian, writing around 94 BC, several centuries later. In it, King Helü has read Sun Wu's thirteen chapters and asks whether he can test the theory on the palace women. Sun Wu divides 180 women into two companies, appoints the king's two favourite concubines as their captains, and explains the drill. When he beats the drum, the women only laugh. He explains again; they laugh again. Sun Wu declares that if orders are clear and not obeyed, the fault lies with the officers, and has the two captains executed, despite the king's protests. After that, the women carry out every command in perfect silence. The king, though grieving, made him a general.
Sima Qian adds that under Sun Wu's command Wu defeated the powerful state of Chu, captured its capital Ying in 506 BC, and made its name feared among the other states.

Historians debate whether Sun Wu existed as described. Older Chinese records of the period do not mention him, and the text of The Art of War, as we have it, seems to reflect warfare of the later Warring States period, the fifth and fourth centuries BC, with large conscript armies and professional generals. Many scholars think the book grew over time as a collection of teachings attached to a famous name.

In 1972 archaeologists opening a Han dynasty tomb at Yinqueshan in Shandong found bamboo strips from around 140 BC carrying a large part of the text, along with a separate work by Sun Bin, a later strategist said to be his descendant. The find showed that the book was already established in the form we know more than two thousand years ago.

The Art of War is short, just thirteen chapters, written in brief, memorable lines. War, it says, is a matter of life and death for the state and must be studied with care. Its most famous ideas include:

that the best victory is to defeat the enemy without fighting at all; that all warfare is based on deception; that one should know the enemy and know oneself, and so not be in danger in a hundred battles; that speed, surprise and the shape of the terrain decide outcomes; and that a skilled commander first makes himself invincible and then waits for the enemy to become vulnerable.

The book was studied by generals and statesmen across East Asia for centuries. It reached Europe in 1772 through a French translation by the Jesuit missionary Jean Joseph Marie Amiot. The British sinologist Lionel Giles published the classic English translation in 1910, which is now in the public domain. Today it is read by business leaders, athletes and coaches as much as by soldiers.

Like the Stoics, Sun Tzu teaches calm judgment under pressure and the importance of preparing what is in your control before acting. No portrait from his lifetime exists; the image on his coin is a modern statue of Sun Tzu in Yurihama, Japan.

name: Niccolò Machiavelli
bio: Florentine diplomat and official who, after losing office and being tortured, wrote The Prince and the Discourses on Livy in exile. He described politics as it is rather than as it should be, which made his name a byword for cunning.

p: Niccolò Machiavelli was born on 3 May 1469 in Florence, the son of Bernardo Machiavelli, a lawyer with a small income and a large love of books. Niccolò received a humanist education in Latin and read the Roman historians closely, above all Livy. He grew up in the Florence of Lorenzo de' Medici and saw the city's fortunes turn after Lorenzo's death in 1492.

In 1494 the Medici were driven out, and for four years the preacher Girolamo Savonarola dominated Florentine politics, until he was executed in 1498. Within weeks, the twenty-nine-year-old Machiavelli was appointed Second Chancellor of the Republic and secretary to the Ten of War, the committee in charge of foreign affairs and defence.

For fourteen years he worked as a diplomat and administrator. He was sent on missions to King Louis XII of France, to the Emperor Maximilian, to Pope Julius II and, most memorably, to Cesare Borgia in 1502 and 1503. He watched Borgia carve out a state in central Italy with speed, cunning and ruthlessness, and later used him as a model in The Prince. Machiavelli also persuaded Florence to raise its own militia instead of relying on mercenaries, and in 1509 that militia helped recapture Pisa.

In 1512 Spanish troops restored the Medici to power and the Republic collapsed. Machiavelli lost his post. Early in 1513 his name was found on a list of suspected conspirators against the Medici. He was arrested and tortured with the strappado, being hoisted by his wrists tied behind his back and dropped. He admitted nothing. Weeks later, when Giovanni de' Medici became Pope Leo X, an amnesty set him free.

He retired to his small farm at Sant'Andrea in Percussina outside Florence. In a famous letter to his friend Francesco Vettori, dated 10 December 1513, he described his days: trapping birds, arguing with woodcutters, playing cards at the inn. In the evening, he wrote, he took off his muddy clothes, put on the robes of court, and entered the company of the ancient writers, who answered him kindly. In those hours he wrote The Prince.

The Prince, finished in 1513 and published only in 1532, after his death, is a short handbook on how to gain and keep power. It argues that a ruler must be willing to act against conventional morality when the survival of the state demands it, and that it is safer to be feared than loved, if one cannot be both. His longer Discourses on Livy praise republics and the civic virtue of ancient Rome. He also wrote The Art of War, a comedy called The Mandrake that is still performed, and the Florentine Histories, commissioned by Cardinal Giulio de' Medici.

A theme of The Prince speaks directly to Stoic readers. Machiavelli writes that fortune is the arbiter of perhaps half our actions, but leaves the other half to us. Fortune is like a flooding river: it cannot be stopped once it rises, but in calm times a wise person builds dykes and embankments. What matters is virtù, energy, skill and readiness to act.

In 1527 the Medici were driven out again and the Republic was restored, but the new government did not trust Machiavelli because he had worked for the Medici. He died a few weeks later, on 21 June 1527, and was buried in the church of Santa Croce in Florence. The portrait on his coin is by Santi di Tito, painted later in the sixteenth century.

name: Epicurus
bio: Founder of the Garden in Athens, the great rival school of the Stoa. He taught that pleasure, understood as freedom from pain and fear, is the goal of life, and that it is best found in simple living and friendship. Seneca quotes him often and with respect.

p: Epicurus was born in 341 BC on the island of Samos, where his Athenian parents had settled as colonists. His father Neocles was a schoolteacher. According to one story, Epicurus turned to philosophy at fourteen, when his teacher could not explain to him what the "chaos" was from which, according to Hesiod, everything came.

He studied with Nausiphanes, a follower of Democritus' atomic theory, and at eighteen went to Athens for his military service. When the Athenian colonists were expelled from Samos in 322 BC, his family moved to Colophon on the coast of Asia Minor, and Epicurus joined them.

Epicurus began teaching in Mytilene on Lesbos and in Lampsacus on the Hellespont. Around 307 BC he moved to Athens and bought a house with a garden outside the city walls, where he lived and taught for the rest of his life. The school became known simply as the Garden.

Unusually for the time, the Garden welcomed women and slaves. Among its members were the courtesan and philosopher Leontion and Themista of Lampsacus, as well as Epicurus' slave Mys. The community lived simply and valued friendship above almost everything else. Over the gate, a later writer says, was the invitation: "Stranger, here you will do well to stay; here the highest good is pleasure."

Epicurus taught that pleasure is the goal of life, which his enemies twisted into a doctrine of indulgence. In fact, he meant something close to the opposite. The highest pleasure, he argued, is the absence of pain in the body and of disturbance in the mind, ataraxia. Most of our troubles come from desires that are neither natural nor necessary, such as fame, luxury and power. He lived mostly on bread and water and once wrote to a friend: "Send me a little pot of cheese, so that I can have a feast whenever I like."
His teaching was summed up later as the "four-part cure": the gods are not to be feared; death is nothing to fear; what is good is easy to get; what is terrible is easy to endure.

life.h: Atoms and the fear of death
p: Following Democritus, Epicurus held that everything is made of atoms moving in empty space. The soul too is made of atoms and scatters at death. "Death is nothing to us," he wrote, "since when we exist, death is not present, and when death is present, we no longer exist." The gods exist, but live in perfect calm and take no interest in human affairs.

Epicurus is said to have written about three hundred works. Almost all are lost. Diogenes Laertius preserved three of his letters, to Herodotus, Pythocles and Menoeceus, and his Principal Doctrines, forty key sayings. Another collection, the Vatican Sayings, was found in a manuscript in 1888. His Roman follower Lucretius set out his philosophy in the great Latin poem On the Nature of Things.

Epicurus died in 270 BC after a long, painful illness from kidney stones. In his last letter he wrote that on this happy day, which was also the last of his life, his pain was extreme, but against it he set the joy of remembering his conversations with his friends.

life.h: Rival and teacher of the Stoics
p: The Stoics and Epicureans were the great rival schools of the Hellenistic world: one built life on virtue, the other on pleasure. Yet Seneca quotes Epicurus in many of his early letters to Lucilius, saying he is happy to borrow good ideas from the enemy camp, and Marcus Aurelius also cites him with respect.

name: Plutarch
bio: Greek biographer, essayist and priest at Delphi. His Parallel Lives pairs famous Greeks and Romans to draw out their character, and his Moralia collects essays on how to live. Much of what we know about Cato the Younger comes from him.

p: Plutarch was born around AD 46 in Chaeronea, a small town in Boeotia in central Greece, where Philip II of Macedon had once defeated the Athenians and Thebans. His family was prosperous and long established there. Plutarch loved his hometown and chose to live there most of his life, joking that he stayed so that it would not become smaller by one more citizen.

Around AD 66 he studied in Athens with the Platonist philosopher Ammonius, and Platonism remained his own philosophy for life. He travelled to Egypt and several times to Rome, where he lectured and made influential friends. Through one of them, the consular Lucius Mestrius Florus, he received Roman citizenship and the name Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus.

He married Timoxena, and they had at least four sons and a daughter. When their two-year-old daughter, also called Timoxena, died while Plutarch was away, he wrote his wife a letter of consolation that survives. It is one of the most moving documents of ancient family life, gentle and practical, reminding her of the joy the child brought them and urging her not to let grief cancel it.

For roughly the last thirty years of his life Plutarch served as one of the two priests of Apollo at Delphi, the most famous oracle of the Greek world. He took the duty seriously, helped restore the sanctuary at a time when its importance was fading, and wrote several dialogues about the oracle and its meaning. The bust shown on his coin was found at Delphi and is traditionally identified as Plutarch, though that identification is not certain.

Plutarch's most famous work is the Parallel Lives, biographies of famous Greeks and Romans arranged in pairs, such as Alexander and Julius Caesar, or Demosthenes and Cicero. Twenty-three pairs survive, along with four single lives. His aim was not history for its own sake but character: he said that a small act, a word or a joke often reveals more about a person than battles in which thousands die. His Life of Cato the Younger is our main source for Cato's death at Utica.

Plutarch also wrote a large collection of essays and dialogues now called the Moralia, around seventy-eight works. They include On Tranquility of Mind, On the Control of Anger, How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend, On Listening, and On Moral Progress. Several essays attack the Stoics and Epicureans on points of doctrine. Even so, his practical advice on anger, calm and self-improvement often sounds very close to Stoic teaching.

Plutarch died some time after AD 119. In 1579 Thomas North published an English translation of the Lives, based on a French version by Jacques Amyot. Shakespeare used North's Plutarch as the source for Julius Caesar, Antony and Cleopatra and Coriolanus, sometimes copying whole passages into verse. Montaigne called Plutarch his favourite author, and the Lives were read closely by the American founders and many later statesmen.

name: Confucius
bio: Teacher and minor official in the state of Lu whose sayings, collected by his students as the Analects, became the foundation of Chinese ethics. He taught self-cultivation, respect within relationships and governing by virtuous example.

p: Confucius, in Chinese Kongzi or Kong Fuzi, "Master Kong", was born in 551 BC near Qufu in the small state of Lu, in today's Shandong province. His personal name was Kong Qiu. His father, Shuliang He, was an old soldier who died when Confucius was about three, and the boy grew up in poverty with his mother, Yan Zhengzai.

He later said that because he was poor and of humble station in his youth, he became skilled in many menial things. As a young man he worked as a keeper of granaries and of livestock for a noble family. He married at nineteen and had a son and a daughter. Meanwhile he taught himself the rites, music, history and poetry of the early Zhou dynasty, which he regarded as a golden age of good order.

Confucius began to take students and became known for his learning. According to tradition, around the age of fifty he entered the service of the Duke of Lu and rose to high office, possibly as Minister of Crime. At a diplomatic meeting with the more powerful state of Qi at Jiagu in 500 BC, his insistence on correct ritual is said to have shamed Qi into returning territory it had taken from Lu.

His career did not last. Traditional accounts say that Qi, worried by Lu's growing strength, sent the duke a gift of dancing girls and fine horses, and the duke neglected government to enjoy them. Around 497 BC Confucius left Lu in disappointment.

For the next fourteen years Confucius travelled from state to state with a small band of disciples, looking for a ruler who would put his ideas into practice. None did. He was threatened, mistaken for an enemy and at one point nearly starved when he and his followers were trapped between the states of Chen and Cai. When a disciple asked whether a gentleman ever finds himself in such need, Confucius answered that a gentleman holds firm in hardship, while a petty person in hardship loses all restraint.

Around 484 BC, aged nearly seventy, Confucius returned to Lu. He spent his last years teaching and, according to tradition, editing the classic books of poetry, history and ritual. He is said to have had three thousand students, of whom seventy-two mastered his teaching. He outlived his son and his favourite disciple, Yan Hui, whose death left him crying out that heaven had destroyed him. Confucius died in 479 BC.

Confucius wrote no book of his own ideas. His sayings and conversations were collected by his disciples and their students in the Analects. They describe the ideal of the junzi, the exemplary person, who cultivates ren, humaneness or goodness, and li, ritual propriety, and who leads by moral example rather than force. Asked for a single word to guide one's whole life, he offered "reciprocity" and explained: "Do not impose on others what you do not wish for yourself."

He summed up his own life in a famous passage: at fifteen he set his heart on learning, at thirty he stood firm, at forty he had no doubts, at fifty he knew the will of heaven, at sixty his ear was attuned, and at seventy he could follow his heart's desire without overstepping what was right.

Under the Han dynasty in the second century BC, his teachings became the official philosophy of the Chinese state, and they shaped education and government in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for two thousand years. His stress on self-cultivation, duty and steady character has much in common with Stoic ethics. The image on his coin is based on a portrait attributed to the Tang painter Wu Daozi.

name: Friedrich Nietzsche
bio: German philologist turned philosopher. In books such as Thus Spoke Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil he attacked conventional morality and called on people to create their own values. His idea of amor fati, loving one's fate, is close to the Stoic acceptance of what happens.

p: Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was born on 15 October 1844 in Röcken, a village in Prussian Saxony. His father, a Lutheran pastor, died in 1849, when Friedrich was four, and the family moved to Naumburg, where he grew up in a household of women: his mother, his sister Elisabeth, his grandmother and two aunts.
He was a brilliant student at Schulpforta, one of the best boarding schools in Germany, and went on to study theology and then classical philology at Bonn and Leipzig.

His teacher Friedrich Ritschl thought so highly of him that in 1869, at only twenty-four and before he had even completed his doctorate, Nietzsche was appointed professor of classical philology at the University of Basel in Switzerland. During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 he volunteered as a medical orderly. He caught dysentery and diphtheria while caring for wounded soldiers, and his health never fully recovered.

In these years he became a close friend of the composer Richard Wagner. His first book, The Birth of Tragedy (1872), celebrated Wagner's music as a rebirth of the Greek tragic spirit. The friendship later collapsed, and Nietzsche became one of Wagner's sharpest critics.

Nietzsche suffered from severe migraines, eye problems and stomach illness. In 1879 he resigned his professorship with a small pension. For the next ten years he lived a wandering life in rented rooms, spending summers in Sils Maria in the Swiss Alps and winters in Genoa, Nice and Turin. He walked for hours each day and wrote in short bursts, often in aphorisms.

In this decade he wrote almost all of his major works: Human, All Too Human; The Gay Science, in which a madman announces that "God is dead"; Thus Spoke Zarathustra; Beyond Good and Evil; On the Genealogy of Morality; Twilight of the Idols, which contains the line "What does not kill me makes me stronger"; and Ecce Homo, his strange, proud autobiography. Few people read his books during his lifetime.

Nietzsche admired and mocked the Stoics in equal measure. In Beyond Good and Evil he made fun of the Stoic ideal of "living according to nature", arguing that nature is wasteful and indifferent, and that the Stoics were really imposing their own ideals on it. Yet his own central formula, amor fati, love of fate, sounds deeply Stoic: "I want to learn more and more to see as beautiful what is necessary in things." He wanted not just to accept what happens but to love it, and to want nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity.

In January 1889, in Turin, Nietzsche suffered a complete mental breakdown. A famous but unverified story says it began when he threw his arms around a horse being beaten in the street. He never recovered. He was cared for first by his mother and then by his sister Elisabeth, and died in Weimar on 25 August 1900.

Elisabeth, an ardent nationalist and antisemite, took control of his papers, edited them to suit her own views and later welcomed the Nazis, who used a distorted version of his work for their purposes. After the Second World War, scholars restored the original texts. Today Nietzsche is recognised as one of the most influential thinkers of the modern age. The photograph on his coin was taken in Naumburg in 1882 by Gustav Schultze.
